Hatchlings of the Scaly thrush emerge from eggs incubated at 38 °C [T = 38 °C] after a period averaging 14 days [ab = 14 days], a value typical for thrushes of this genus and comparable to that documented in the closely related Ring ouzel, Turdus torquatus. At the point of hatching, these altricial nestlings possess an initial wet body mass of approximately 8.975 grams [Ww0 = approximately 8.975 grams]. This low birth weight, characteristic of altricial birds, necessitates an extended period of intense biparental provisioning. The nestling phase is defined by rapid feather development and a steep increase in body mass, as the growing chick transitions from reliance on yolk reserves to a diet of invertebrates provided by the attending adults. The precise control of incubation temperature is critical during this early stage, as deviations can profoundly affect hatching success and subsequent chick viability. Field observations indicate that the thermal environment of the nest, closely regulated by the incubating parent, is maintained near this optimal 38 °C [T = 38 °C] for the majority of the incubation period.

Under the sustained thermal regime of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], which approximates the typical core body temperature of an incubating or brooding adult during active metabolic periods, the Scaly thrush displays a consistent sequence of developmental events. Fledging, defined as the age at which the nestling achieves its first sustained flight, occurs at 14 days after hatching [tx = 14 days after hatching], a milestone again inferred from life-history data for Turdus torquatus at a temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. This relatively rapid transition to flight capability is crucial for evading nest predation. Following fledging, the juvenile enters a period of sexual maturation, with puberty attained at 42 days after hatching [tp = 42 days after hatching] at a temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. This relatively brief juvenile stage for a bird of moderate size suggests a life-history strategy that prioritizes early reproductive opportunity. The high metabolic demand required to fuel this rapid growth and development is reflected in a maximal basal metabolic rate of 143.11 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 143.11 milliliters of oxygen per hour] when measured at 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], a figure that underscores the elevated energetic costs of tissue synthesis and thermoregulation in this species.

Sexual dimorphism in body size becomes evident as individuals approach their ultimate mass. Adult females attain a maximum wet body weight of 141.5 grams [Wwi = 141.5 grams], while males are slightly larger, reaching an ultimate wet weight of 150 grams [Wwi = 150 grams]. This size difference, where males are the heavier sex, is a common pattern among thrushes and may relate to advantages in territorial defense or competition for mates. The divergence likely manifests during the latter stages of the juvenile growth phase, after the nutritional demands of rapid feather development have subsided. Attainment of this adult mass is a prerequisite for successful reproduction, ensuring that individuals have sufficient somatic reserves to sustain the energetic costs of egg production and the demanding period of provisioning nestlings. The maximum body mass, particularly in males, correlates with dominance hierarchies on the breeding grounds, where heavier males are often more successful at securing high-quality territories with abundant food resources for their broods.

At a sustained temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], the first successful brood is typically produced at 1.2 years after birth [tR = 1.2 years after birth], representing the onset of effective reproductive activity. This relatively early age at first reproduction, following closely upon the attainment of puberty, suggests a life-history strategy geared toward high annual fecundity in suitable habitats. The maximum annual reproductive output is substantial, with females capable of producing a total of 3.75 eggs per year [Ri = 3.75 eggs per year]. This annual rate is achieved through the production of multiple clutches, a strategy that compensates for potential nest failure, a common occurrence for ground-nesting songbirds exposed to a variety of predators. The total number of eggs produced annually is directly tied to the availability of invertebrate prey during the breeding season, with years of high food abundance often correlating with larger clutch sizes and a higher frequency of nesting attempts within the population.

The species is not particularly long-lived for a passerine of its body size; the maximum documented lifespan under these thermal conditions (40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]) is approximately 8.6 years [am = approximately 8.6 years]. This relatively shorter lifespan, in concert with the high annual reproductive rate, points to a life-history strategy characterized by a fast turnover of generations. Mortality is highest during the first year of life, particularly in the period immediately following fledging and independence, when juveniles must learn to forage effectively and evade predators without parental guidance. Those individuals that survive this critical bottleneck and establish a territory can expect to breed for several seasons, though reproductive output typically declines in the final years of life as senescence takes its toll on physiological condition and foraging efficiency.
